prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We provide a new estimate of the local supermassive black hole mass function using (i) the empirical relation between supermassive black hole mass and the Sersic index of the host spheroidal stellar system and (ii) the measured (spheroid) Sersic indices drawn from 10k galaxies in the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue. The observational simplicity of our approach, and the direct measurements of the black hole predictor quantity, i.e. the Sersic index, for both elliptical galaxies and the bulges of disc galaxies makes it straightforward to estimate accurate black hole masses in early- and late-type galaxies alike. We have parameterised the supermassive black hole mass function with a Schechter function and find, at the low-mass end, a logarithmic slope (1+alpha) of ~0.7 for the full galaxy sample and ~1.0 for the early-type galaxy sample. Considering spheroidal stellar systems brighter than M_B = -18 mag, and integrating down to black hole masses of 10^6 M_sun, we find that the local mass density of supermassive black holes in early-type galaxies rho_{bh, early-type} = (3.5+/-1.2) x 10^5 h^3_{70} M_sun Mpc^{-3}, and in late-type galaxies rho_{bh, late-type} = (1.0+/-0.5) x 10^5 h^3_{70} M_sun Mpc^{-3}. The uncertainties are derived from Monte Carlo simulations which include uncertainties in the M_bh-n relation, the catalogue of Sersic indices, the galaxy weights and Malmquist bias. The combined, cosmological, supermassive black hole mass density is thus Omega_{bh, total} = (3.2+/-1.2) x 10^{-6} h_70. That is, using a new and independent method, we conclude that (0.007+/-0.003) h^3_{70} per cent of the universe's baryons are presently locked up in supermassive black holes at the centres of galaxies.

We provide a new estimate of the local supermassive black hole mass function using (i) the empirical relation between supermassive black hole mass and the Sérsic index of the host spheroidal stellar system, and (ii) the measured spheroid Sérsic indices drawn from 10k galaxies in the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue. The observational simplicity of our approach, together with the direct measurement of the black hole predictor quantity—namely, the Sérsic index—for both elliptical galaxies and the bulges of disc galaxies, makes it straightforward to estimate accurate black hole masses in early- and late-type galaxies alike.

We have parameterised the supermassive black hole mass function with a Schechter function and find, at the low-mass end, a logarithmic slope \((1+\alpha)\) of \(\sim 0.7\) for the full galaxy sample and \(\sim 1.0\) for the early-type galaxy sample. Considering spheroidal stellar systems brighter than \(M_B = -18\) mag, and integrating down to black hole masses of \(10^6 M_\odot\), we find that the local mass density of supermassive black holes in early-type galaxies is \(\rho_{\rm bh, early-type} = (3.5 \pm 1.2) \times 10^5 h^3_{70} M_\odot\,{\rm Mpc}^{-3}\), while that in late-type galaxies is \(\rho_{\rm bh, late-type} = (1.0 \pm 0.5) \times 10^5 h^3_{70} M_\odot\,{\rm Mpc}^{-3}\).

The uncertainties are derived from Monte Carlo simulations that include uncertainties in the \(M_{\rm bh}\)-\(n\) relation, the catalogue of Sérsic indices, the galaxy weights, and Malmquist bias. The combined cosmological supermassive black hole mass density is therefore \(\Omega_{\rm bh, total} = (3.2 \pm 1.2) \times 10^{-6} h_{70}\). Thus, using a new and independent method, we conclude that \((0.007 \pm 0.003) h^3_{70}\) per cent of the universe’s baryons are presently locked up in supermassive black holes at the centres of galaxies.

We present a revised determination of the local mass function of supermassive black holes, based on two inputs: (i) the observed correlation between supermassive black hole mass and the Sérsic index of the surrounding spheroidal stellar component, and (ii) spheroid Sérsic index measurements obtained from 10,000 galaxies in the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue.

Because this method relies on relatively simple observations and uses direct measurements of the black-hole predictor—the Sérsic index—for both elliptical galaxies and the bulges of disc galaxies, it provides a clear way to infer black hole masses reliably in both early- and late-type systems.

We describe the supermassive black hole mass function with a Schechter function. At the low-mass end, we obtain a logarithmic slope, \(1+\alpha\), of approximately 0.7 for the complete galaxy sample and about 1.0 for the early-type galaxy subset.

Restricting the analysis to spheroidal stellar systems brighter than \(M_B = -18\) mag and integrating the mass function down to black hole masses of \(10^6\,M_\odot\), we estimate the present-day mass density of supermassive black holes to be

\[
\rho_{\mathrm{bh,early-type}} = (3.5 \pm 1.2) \times 10^5\, h_{70}^3\, M_\odot\, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}
\]

for early-type galaxies, and

\[
\rho_{\mathrm{bh,late-type}} = (1.0 \pm 0.5) \times 10^5\, h_{70}^3\, M_\odot\, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}
\]

for late-type galaxies.

The quoted errors come from Monte Carlo simulations that account for uncertainties in the \(M_{\mathrm{bh}}-n\) relation, the Sérsic-index catalogue, galaxy weighting factors, and Malmquist bias.

Combining the contributions from all galaxy types gives a cosmological supermassive black hole mass density of

\[
\Omega_{\mathrm{bh,total}} = (3.2 \pm 1.2) \times 10^{-6}\, h_{70}.
\]

Thus, using an independent new approach, we infer that \((0.007 \pm 0.003)\,h_{70}^3\) per cent of the baryonic matter in the Universe is currently contained in supermassive black holes located at galactic centres.

The study estimates the local supermassive black hole mass function by using the observed relationship between a black hole’s mass and the Sérsic index of its host galaxy’s spheroidal component. Since the Sérsic index describes the concentration and shape of a galaxy’s light profile, it provides a way to infer black hole masses from galaxy structure, even when direct dynamical measurements are not available.

To carry out this analysis, the study uses measured spheroid Sérsic indices for approximately 10,000 galaxies from the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue. These galaxies include both early-type systems, such as elliptical and lenticular galaxies, and late-type systems, such as spiral galaxies with central bulges. By applying the black hole mass–Sérsic index relation to the spheroidal components of these galaxies, the authors estimate the masses of the central supermassive black holes across the local galaxy population.

The resulting supermassive black hole mass function is described using a Schechter function, a common parameterisation for astronomical mass and luminosity distributions. This fit gives a low-mass-end logarithmic slope of approximately 0.7 for the full galaxy sample. When only early-type galaxies are considered, the slope is steeper, at about 1.0, indicating that the relative abundance of lower-mass black holes differs between galaxy types.

The study also derives the local mass density of supermassive black holes. For early-type galaxies, the estimated black hole mass density is  
\[
(3.5 \pm 1.2) \times 10^5\, h_{70}^3\, M_\odot\, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-3},
\]
while for late-type galaxies it is  
\[
(1.0 \pm 0.5) \times 10^5\, h_{70}^3\, M_\odot\, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}.
\]
These results indicate that early-type galaxies contain the majority of the local mass density in central supermassive black holes, although late-type galaxies also make a significant contribution.

Combining these estimates, the study concludes that  
\[
(0.007 \pm 0.003)\, h_{70}^3
\]
percent of the universe’s baryonic matter is currently locked up in supermassive black holes located at the centers of galaxies. This provides an important constraint on the growth history of black holes and their connection to galaxy evolution in the local universe.

By applying the black hole mass–Sérsic index relation to these galaxies, the authors infer the distribution of black hole masses in the nearby universe.

\]

of all baryons are locked up in supermassive black holes today. outputs.L5:
The **Sérsic profile**, the **Millennium Simulation**, and the study of **galaxy** formation are closely connected in modern astrophysics. Together, they help researchers understand how galaxies form, evolve, and acquire their observed structures.

The **Sérsic profile** is a mathematical function used to describe how the brightness of a galaxy changes with distance from its center. It is commonly written in terms of the Sérsic index, *n*, which indicates the shape of the galaxy’s light distribution. A low Sérsic index, such as *n* ≈ 1, is typical of disk galaxies with exponential light profiles, while a higher value, such as *n* ≈ 4, often describes elliptical galaxies with more centrally concentrated light. By fitting Sérsic profiles to observed galaxies, astronomers can classify their structures and study their formation history.

The **Millennium Simulation** is one of the most important cosmological simulations ever created. It follows the growth of dark matter structures in a large volume of the universe over cosmic time. Although the simulation primarily models dark matter, it can be combined with semi-analytic models to predict the formation and evolution of galaxies within dark matter halos. These models allow scientists to compare simulated galaxies with real observations.

In galaxy research, Sérsic measurements provide a bridge between observations and simulations like the Millennium Simulation. Observers can measure Sérsic indices, sizes, and luminosities of galaxies in large sky surveys, while theorists can use simulations to predict how galaxies should look at different stages of cosmic evolution. Comparing these results helps test theories of galaxy formation, including the roles of mergers, gas cooling, star formation, and feedback from supernovae or active galactic nuclei.

For example, a galaxy that has experienced many mergers may develop a high Sérsic index and resemble an elliptical galaxy. In contrast, a galaxy that grows more quietly by accreting gas may maintain a disk-like structure with a low Sérsic index. The Millennium Simulation provides a framework for tracing these histories, while Sérsic profile fitting helps quantify the visible structure of the galaxies produced.

In this way, the concepts of **Sérsic**, **Millennium**, and **galaxy** come together to form an important part of contemporary cosmology. They allow astronomers to connect the large-scale structure of the universe with the detailed shapes and brightness profiles of individual galaxies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for an astrophysics paper estimating the local supermassive black hole mass function from the M_bh–Sersic index relation using Millennium Galaxy Catalogue data.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

We estimate the local supermassive black hole (SMBH) mass function using the empirical correlation between black hole mass, \(M_{\rm bh}\), and host-spheroid Sérsic index, \(n\), applied to the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue (MGC). The MGC provides a deep, high-quality, \(B\)-band structural decomposition of nearby galaxies, enabling the spheroid component and its Sérsic index to be measured across a statistically useful local volume. We combine these measurements with the calibrated \(M_{\rm bh}\)–\(n\) relation to assign black hole masses to spheroids and construct the \(z \simeq 0\) SMBH mass function, accounting for survey selection effects, galaxy weights, and the intrinsic scatter in the scaling relation. The resulting mass function is dominated in number by black holes with masses \(M_{\rm bh}\sim10^{6}–10^{8}\,M_\odot\), while the integrated black hole mass density is primarily contributed by systems near and above \(10^{8}\,M_\odot\). We find a local SMBH mass density of order a few \(10^{5}\,M_\odot\,{\rm Mpc}^{-3}\), consistent with estimates based on the \(M_{\rm bh}\)–\(\sigma\) and \(M_{\rm bh}\)–bulge luminosity relations, as well as with constraints from the integrated quasar luminosity density. The \(M_{\rm bh}\)–Sérsic index method provides an independent route to the local black hole census and is particularly valuable because it relies on host-galaxy light-profile shape rather than velocity dispersion or luminosity alone. Our results support a close connection between SMBH growth and the structural evolution of galaxy spheroids, and demonstrate that Sérsic-index-based estimates can provide a robust complementary probe of the local black hole population.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study that derives the local SMBH mass density in early- and late-type galaxies using spheroid Sersic indices and a Schechter-function black hole mass function.
counterfactuals.output:
The study estimated the **local supermassive black hole (SMBH) mass density** separately for **early-type** and **late-type galaxies** by using the structural properties of galaxy spheroids—specifically their **Sérsic indices**—to infer black hole masses.

### Core idea

Instead of deriving SMBH masses from bulge luminosity or stellar velocity dispersion, the authors used the empirical relation between SMBH mass and spheroid Sérsic index:

\[
M_{\rm BH} \;-\; n_{\rm sph}
\]

where \(n_{\rm sph}\) describes the concentration of the spheroid light profile. More centrally concentrated spheroids tend to host more massive black holes.

### Method

1. **Galaxy sample**
   - The study used a local galaxy survey with morphological classifications and bulge–disc decompositions.
   - Galaxies were separated into:
     - **Early-type systems**: ellipticals and lenticulars.
     - **Late-type systems**: spirals with spheroidal bulges.

2. **Sérsic-index measurements**
   - For each spheroid, the Sérsic index \(n\) was used to estimate the central black hole mass through an empirical \(M_{\rm BH}-n\) relation.

3. **Black hole mass function**
   - The resulting distribution of black hole masses was described with a **Schechter-like black hole mass function**, analogous to the Schechter luminosity function used for galaxies.
   - Integrating this function over black hole mass gave the SMBH mass density.

### Main results

The study found a total local SMBH mass density of roughly

\[
\rho_{\rm BH} \approx 3.8 \times 10^{5}\; M_\odot\,{\rm Mpc}^{-3}
\]

for the nearby Universe.

Broken down by host type:

- **Early-type galaxies** contribute about

\[
\rho_{\rm BH,early} \approx 2.9 \times 10^{5}\; M_\odot\,{\rm Mpc}^{-3}
\]

- **Late-type galaxies** contribute about

\[
\rho_{\rm BH,late} \approx 0.9 \times 10^{5}\; M_\odot\,{\rm Mpc}^{-3}
\]

Thus, approximately **three-quarters of the local SMBH mass density resides in early-type galaxies**, while about **one-quarter resides in late-type galaxies**.

### Interpretation

The result supports the view that most of the black hole mass in the local Universe is locked up in massive spheroids, especially ellipticals and lenticulars. Late-type galaxies are numerous, but their bulges are typically less concentrated and host lower-mass black holes, so their contribution to the total SMBH mass density is smaller.

### Significance

This approach was important because it provided an independent estimate of the local SMBH mass function and mass density using **spheroid structure** rather than only velocity dispersion or luminosity. The derived density was broadly consistent with estimates based on quasar light and accretion-history arguments, supporting the idea that most SMBH growth occurred through radiatively efficient accretion during active galactic phases.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise journal-style abstract describing a new independent method for calculating the cosmological supermassive black hole mass density from 10k galaxies in the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

We present an independent determination of the local cosmological supermassive black hole mass density using a sample of ∼10,000 galaxies from the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue. Rather than inferring black hole growth from integrated quasar light or adopting a single galaxy luminosity function, our method estimates black hole masses on a galaxy-by-galaxy basis by combining structural bulge–disc decompositions with empirical black-hole–host-galaxy scaling relations. Bulge luminosities and stellar masses are corrected for selection effects, incompleteness, and survey volume, allowing construction of the local black hole mass function and direct integration to obtain the mass density. We find a present-day supermassive black hole mass density of order \(\rho_{\rm BH} \simeq (3–5)\times10^{5}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm Mpc}^{-3}\), consistent with estimates from quasar accretion histories but derived through an entirely independent census of nearby galaxies. The dominant uncertainties arise from the intrinsic scatter and calibration of black-hole scaling relations, bulge–disc decomposition systematics, and stellar mass-to-light ratios. This approach provides a robust low-redshift benchmark for models of black hole growth and galaxy co-evolution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical astronomy abstract including numerical results for rho_bh in early-type and late-type galaxies, Omega_bh,total, Monte Carlo uncertainty estimates, and the role of the M_bh–n relation.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract** — We estimate the local supermassive black hole mass density by combining galaxy luminosity functions, bulge/disc decompositions, Sérsic-index distributions, and the empirical \(M_{\rm bh}\)–\(n\) relation between black hole mass and bulge Sérsic index. Treating early-type galaxies as spheroid-dominated systems and late-type galaxies as disc systems hosting classical/pseudo-bulges, we derive separate contributions to the black hole mass density, \(\rho_{\rm bh}\). For early-type galaxies we find

\[
\rho_{\rm bh,early} = (3.1 \pm 0.6)\times 10^{5}\ M_{\odot}\ {\rm Mpc}^{-3},
\]

while late-type galaxies contribute

\[
\rho_{\rm bh,late} = (1.2 \pm 0.4)\times 10^{5}\ M_{\odot}\ {\rm Mpc}^{-3}.
\]

The total local black hole mass density is therefore

\[
\rho_{\rm bh,total} = (4.3 \pm 0.8)\times 10^{5}\ M_{\odot}\ {\rm Mpc}^{-3},
\]

corresponding to a cosmological density parameter

\[
\Omega_{\rm bh,total}
= \frac{\rho_{\rm bh,total}}{\rho_{\rm crit}}
= (3.2 \pm 0.6)\times 10^{-6},
\]

for \(H_{0}=70\ {\rm km\ s^{-1}\ Mpc^{-1}}\) and \(\rho_{\rm crit}=1.36\times 10^{11}\ M_{\odot}\ {\rm Mpc}^{-3}\). Monte Carlo propagation of uncertainties in the luminosity functions, bulge-to-total ratios, Sérsic-index distributions, intrinsic scatter in the \(M_{\rm bh}\)–\(n\) relation, and morphological fractions yields a fractional uncertainty of \(\simeq 19\%\) on the total density. The simulations indicate that early-type galaxies dominate the local black hole mass budget, contributing approximately \(72\%\) of \(\rho_{\rm bh,total}\), with late-type bulges supplying the remaining \(28\%\).

The \(M_{\rm bh}\)–\(n\) relation is central to this estimate because it provides a structural, rather than purely luminosity- or velocity-dispersion-based, route to assigning black hole masses to galaxy bulges. Its use is particularly important for late-type galaxies, where bulge luminosities and velocity dispersions are more uncertain and where low-\(n\) bulges contribute significantly to the number density but only modestly to the integrated mass density. Our results are consistent with independent estimates based on the \(M_{\rm bh}\)–\(\sigma\) and \(M_{\rm bh}\)–\(M_{\rm bulge}\) relations, supporting a local black hole density of order \(4\times 10^{5}\ M_{\odot}\ {\rm Mpc}^{-3}\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a research-paper abstract about estimating black hole masses in elliptical galaxies and disc-galaxy bulges via directly measured Sersic indices, with results integrated down to 10^6 solar masses.
counterfactuals.output:
We present a homogeneous calibration and application of the black hole mass–Sérsic index relation for elliptical galaxies and the bulges of disc galaxies, using directly measured Sérsic indices rather than values inferred from luminosity, stellar mass, or velocity dispersion. Structural parameters were obtained from multi-component surface-brightness decompositions that separate bulges from discs, bars, lenses, rings, and nuclear components, enabling consistent estimates of the Sérsic index \(n\) for both pressure-supported ellipticals and embedded bulges. Combining these measurements with galaxies hosting dynamically measured black hole masses, we recalibrate the \(M_{\rm BH}\)–\(n\) relation and quantify its intrinsic scatter over the full range of spheroid concentration.

The resulting relation confirms that black hole mass correlates strongly with spheroid light concentration, with higher Sérsic indices corresponding to more massive central black holes. When applied to a broader sample of early-type galaxies and disc-galaxy bulges, the relation yields black hole mass estimates spanning from giant ellipticals to low-mass spheroids. By integrating the inferred distribution down to \(M_{\rm BH}=10^{6}\,M_{\odot}\), we obtain an updated census of the local massive black hole population that includes systems typically missed by samples limited to high luminosities or large velocity dispersions.

Our results indicate that directly measured Sérsic indices provide a practical route to estimating black hole masses in galaxies lacking spatially resolved dynamical measurements, particularly for low- and intermediate-mass bulges. The inclusion of disc-galaxy bulges substantially increases the predicted number density of black holes near \(10^{6}\)–\(10^{7}\,M_{\odot}\), highlighting the importance of careful bulge/disc decomposition in black hole demographic studies. These findings support the use of Sérsic-based scaling relations as a complementary tool for mapping the low-mass end of the black hole mass function and for connecting black hole growth to the structural evolution of galactic spheroids.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
